grammar.name: Complex relative clauses with quantifiers
grammar.rule: This adds extra, non-essential information by combining a quantity word (like 'many' or 'most') with 'of which' or 'of whom'.

grammar.tip: Always put a comma before this structure, because the extra information is not essential. Never use 'that' instead of 'which' or 'whom' here.

grammar.name: Concession: despite/in spite of + noun/-ing vs. although + clause
grammar.rule: This shows a contrast, but the grammar after it depends on the connector you choose. Use a noun or an -ing phrase after 'despite'/'in spite of'. Use a full clause after 'although'/'even though'.
grammar.formula: Despite/In spite of + noun/-ing, clause. | Although/Even though + clause, clause.
grammar.example: Despite growing awareness of globalisation and trade, meaningful action has been slow to materialise.
grammar.tip: Never put a subject + verb clause right after 'despite' or 'in spite of'. This is one of the most common mistakes at B2 level.

grammar.name: Emphatic do / so...that / such...that
grammar.rule: The word 'do' can add extra stress to a verb, often to correct or contrast something. 'So...that' and 'such...that' make a description stronger and show its result.
grammar.formula: Subject + do/does/did + base verb | so + adj/adv + that-clause | such + (a/an) + adj + noun + that-clause
grammar.example: The evidence on globalisation and trade was so compelling that even sceptical policymakers took notice.
grammar.tip: Use emphatic 'do' only for real contrast or correction. If you use it too often, it loses its effect.

grammar.tip: The person or thing doing the -ing action must be the same as the subject of the main sentence. Otherwise, the meaning becomes unclear.

grammar.name: Perfect participle clauses (sequence)
grammar.rule: This shows that one action finished before another one started. It puts both actions into one shorter clause.
grammar.formula: Having + past participle, main clause.
grammar.example: Having reviewed the evidence on media, advertising and social media, the committee revised its original recommendations.
grammar.tip: Use 'having + past participle' (not just '-ing') whenever the order of events is important.

grammar.name: Passive with reporting verbs
grammar.rule: This structure makes a claim sound more neutral and less personal. It is common in academic writing and in Task 2 essays.
grammar.formula: It + is/was + past participle (reporting verb) + that-clause
grammar.example: It is widely believed that crime, law and punishment will remain a defining issue for the next generation.
grammar.tip: Do not use this structure too many times in one paragraph. Mix it with active sentences so your writing does not sound repetitive.

grammar.name: Causative passive (have/get something done)
grammar.rule: This describes asking or paying someone else to do something for you, instead of doing it yourself.
grammar.formula: have/get + object + past participle
grammar.example: Many local authorities have had independent studies conducted into crime, law and punishment.
grammar.tip: This is different from a simple passive sentence. The causative shows that the subject arranged the action — not just that it happened to them.

grammar.name: Mandative subjunctive
grammar.rule: This is used after words like recommend, insist, essential, or vital — words that show a recommendation, a demand, or a necessity.
grammar.formula: Subject + suggest/recommend/insist + that + subject + base verb (no -s, no tense change)
grammar.example: Experts recommend that policy on crime, law and punishment be reviewed on an annual basis.
grammar.tip: The verb after 'that' always stays in its base form. It never changes for person or tense: use 'be reviewed', not 'is reviewed' or 'was reviewed'.

grammar.name: Complex relative clauses with quantifiers
grammar.rule: This adds extra, non-essential information by combining a quantity word (like 'many' or 'most') with 'of which' or 'of whom'.
grammar.formula: ..., [quantifier] of which/whom + clause
grammar.example: The survey included 1,200 respondents, the majority of whom expressed concern about crime, law and punishment.
grammar.tip: Always put a comma before this structure, because the extra information is not essential. Never use 'that' instead of 'which' or 'whom' here.

grammar.name: Reduced relative clauses
grammar.rule: This leaves out the relative pronoun (like 'that' or 'which') and the auxiliary verb. It makes the sentence shorter and more academic.
grammar.formula: Noun + [participle clause] (no relative pronoun)
grammar.example: Measures aimed at addressing crime, law and punishment require sustained political commitment to succeed.
grammar.tip: You can only shorten a relative clause this way when the pronoun you remove would have been the subject of that clause.

grammar.name: Concession: despite/in spite of + noun/-ing vs. although + clause
grammar.rule: This shows a contrast, but the grammar after it depends on the connector you choose. Use a noun or an -ing phrase after 'despite'/'in spite of'. Use a full clause after 'although'/'even though'.
grammar.formula: Despite/In spite of + noun/-ing, clause. | Although/Even though + clause, clause.
grammar.example: Despite growing awareness of crime, law and punishment, meaningful action has been slow to materialise.
grammar.tip: Never put a subject + verb clause right after 'despite' or 'in spite of'. This is one of the most common mistakes at B2 level.

grammar.name: Emphatic do / so...that / such...that
grammar.rule: The word 'do' can add extra stress to a verb, often to correct or contrast something. 'So...that' and 'such...that' make a description stronger and show its result.
grammar.formula: Subject + do/does/did + base verb | so + adj/adv + that-clause | such + (a/an) + adj + noun + that-clause
grammar.example: The evidence on crime, law and punishment was so compelling that even sceptical policymakers took notice.
grammar.tip: Use emphatic 'do' only for real contrast or correction. If you use it too often, it loses its effect.
